description.en: Teff is a tiny ancient grain native to Ethiopia and Eritrea, where it has been cultivated for thousands of years and remains a dietary staple, most famously as the base for injera flatbread. Despite its small size, it has a rich, slightly sweet, nutty, almost molasses-like flavor. It's typically ground into flour for fermented flatbreads and porridges, or cooked whole as a side grain similar to quinoa. Nutritionally, it's naturally gluten-free and notably high in iron, calcium, and fiber compared to most other grains.

Fresh pepeiao has a convex shape with a smooth, sometimes wrinkly surface, and can be a purply gray-brown color. It has a slightly chewy texture that many describe as rubbery-crunchy. It grows wild on logs of koa and kukui trees in Hawaii, typically on fallen or dying tree branches, often appearing after rain. It's known for its ability to absorb flavors when cooked and is commonly added to soups and stir-fries. It's a staple in Hawaii's Asian-influenced cuisine and is essentially the same category of mushroom used as "wood ear" or "cloud ear" in Chinese and Japanese cooking -sometimes called kikurage-.

BIFIDOBACTERIUM ANIMALIS is a gram-positive, anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium of the Bifidobacterium genus which can be found in the large intestines of humans. Both old names B. animalis and B. lactis are still used on product labels, as this species is frequently used as a probiotic. In most cases, which subspecies is used in the product is not clear. Several companies have attempted to trademark particular strains, and as a marketing technique, have invented scientific-sounding names for the strains.

description.en: Juice is the liquid extracted from fruits or vegetables, produced by pressing, squeezing, or blending, with a history stretching back to ancient civilizations that fermented or drank fruit juices, though modern commercial juicing scaled up dramatically in the 20th century with pasteurization and packaging advances. It has a flavor that mirrors its source—sweet, tart, or a mix—with a smooth, liquid texture, sometimes with pulp retained for added body. description.en: Fructose is a simple sugar -monosaccharide- that occurs naturally in fruits, honey, and some vegetables, and is produced commercially either by processing corn starch into high-fructose corn syrup -mainly in the U.S.- or by refining it from sucrose. It has the sweetest taste of all natural sugars—notably sweeter than sucrose or glucose—with no notable aroma, and is used in beverages, baked goods, and processed foods both for its intense sweetness and its ability to enhance flavor and browning. Fructose provides purely empty calories with no fiber, vitamins, or minerals, and is metabolized differently than glucose—processed primarily by the liver—which has made it a focus of concern around excessive consumption and links to metabolic issues.

description.en: CHOLINE is a water-soluble vitamin-like essential nutrient. The US Food and Drug Administration requires that infant formula not made from cow's milk be supplemented with choline. Choline-providing dietary supplement ingredients include: choline chloride, choline bitartrate, citicoline -CDP-choline-, L-alpha-glycerophosphocholine -Alpha-GPC-, lecithin, phosphatidylcholine. Cruciferous vegetables, such as Brussels sprouts and broccoli, are good sources of choline.

Native to Mexico and Guatemala, chia seeds come from the flowering plant Salvia hispanica. Black seeds are the traditional, more widely available variety; white seeds are a naturally occurring lighter variant, often prized for their appearance in pale-colored dishes. Both share a mild, nutty flavor and neutral taste, absorbing surrounding flavors easily. When soaked, they develop a gel-like texture, making them ideal for puddings, smoothies, baked goods, and as an egg substitute. Nutritionally identical, both are rich in fiber, plant-based omega-3s, protein, calcium, and antioxidants — a versatile, nutrient-dense addition to any diet.

description.en: Wheat flour comes from wheat, one of the world's oldest cultivated grains, first domesticated in the Fertile Crescent around 10‚000 years ago and now the dominant grain in global bread-making, especially in Europe, the Middle East, and the Americas. It has a mild, slightly sweet, neutral flavor with a texture that ranges from soft and fine -cake flour- to coarse and hearty -whole wheat-, largely defined by its protein and gluten content, which gives dough its characteristic elasticity and chew. Wheat flour contains gluten and, depending on whether it's whole grain or refined, provides varying levels of fiber, B vitamins, iron, and protein—whole wheat retaining significantly more nutrients since the bran and germ aren't stripped away.

description.en: Amaranth seed, pale brown -Amaranthus cruentus-, known regionally as Rajagaro -Gujarati-, Ramdana -Hindi-, and Cavali biya -Marathi-, among other local names. Unlike the deep black-seeded variety, this pale brown form has a milder, subtly sweet, nutty flavor. In Indian cuisine, it's commonly popped and used in fasting foods -vrat ka khana-, ground into flour for flatbreads, or mixed with jaggery to make chikki-style sweets. Nutritionally, it's a good source of plant protein, dietary fiber, iron, and calcium, and is naturally gluten-free—making it a popular grain substitute during religious fasting periods across India.

Melado is an unrefined liquid sugar syrup made from concentrated sugarcane juice, a traditional product especially common in Brazil and other Latin American countries where it's produced as a byproduct or lighter-processed cousin of molasses, retaining more of the cane's natural sweetness. It has a rich, deep caramel flavor with molasses-like notes but milder and less bitter than true molasses, and a thick, syrupy texture. Used in traditional desserts, sauces, and as a spread or sweetener in Brazilian and Latin American cooking, melado retains modest amounts of minerals like calcium, iron, and potassium from the cane juice, making it slightly more nutritious than fully refined sugar.

description.en: Breadfruit is a starchy tropical fruit native to the South Pacific and Southeast Asia, long cultivated across Polynesian islands as a dietary staple, and historically significant for its role in the 18th-century Bounty voyage, which aimed to transplant it to the Caribbean as cheap food for enslaved laborers. It has a mild, slightly sweet flavor reminiscent of fresh bread or potato when cooked, with a starchy, dense texture similar to a potato when roasted, boiled, or fried. Typically eaten cooked rather than raw, breadfruit is a good source of complex carbohydrates, fiber, potassium, and vitamin C, making it a nutrient-dense staple food in many tropical regions.

Pearled barley is barley that has had its outer hull and bran layer removed through a polishing -pearling- process. This distinguishes it from "hulled barley," which only has the inedible outer hull removed and keeps the bran intact. Lower in fiber than hulled barley -since the bran is polished away-. Good source of manganese, selenium, and B vitamins like niacin. Mild, nutty flavor with a pleasantly chewy, slightly sticky texture when cooked — it releases starch similarly to arborio rice, which is why it works well in risotto-style preparations.

description.en: Yeast extract is a savory paste or powder made by breaking down yeast cells—typically through autolysis -self-digestion using the yeast's own enzymes- or hydrolysis—a byproduct process refined in the late 19th century that led to iconic products like Marmite in the UK and Vegemite in Australia. It has an intensely savory, salty, umami-rich flavor with deep, almost meaty notes, and comes as a thick, sticky spread or dried into a fine powder used as a seasoning. Used as a flavor enhancer in soups, sauces, stocks, and spreads, yeast extract is naturally rich in glutamic acid -contributing its umami punch-, B vitamins, and protein, making it both a flavor booster and a modest nutritional contributor.

description.en: Native to Mesoamerica and introduced to India centuries ago, tender local maize -Zea mays- refers to indigenous Indian corn varieties harvested young, while the kernels are still soft and milky rather than fully mature and dried. It has a starchy, mildly sweet, earthy flavor—less sugary than sweet corn but with a satisfying bite. Widely enjoyed as street food, it's traditionally roasted over open coals and rubbed with lime, chili, and salt -bhutta-, boiled as a snack, or grated into curries, soups, and flatbreads. Nutritionally, tender maize provides dietary fiber, complex carbohydrates, and moderate protein, along with B vitamins, magnesium, and antioxidants like lutein and zeaxanthin, making it a wholesome seasonal staple across India.

Cranberries come in two main varieties: the American cranberry -Vaccinium macrocarpon-, native to North America and long used by Indigenous peoples before becoming a major commercial crop in states like Massachusetts and Wisconsin, and the smaller European cranberry -Vaccinium oxycoccos-, native to boggy regions across Northern Europe and Asia and traditionally foraged rather than farmed. Both have a sharply tart, astringent flavor with a firm, crisp bite when fresh, though the European variety tends to be smaller and even more tart than its larger American cousin. Eaten fresh, dried, juiced, or made into sauces, cranberries are notably rich in antioxidants, vitamin C, and compounds linked to urinary tract health, making them valued more for their functional benefits than their raw palatability.

description.en: "Anglerfish" is a broad term for an order of fish -Lophiiformes- known for using a fleshy growth on their head like a fishing lure to attract prey. The fish sold as "monkfish" in seafood markets typically refers to species in the genus Lophius — like the American anglerfish -Lophius americanus- or European anglerfish -Lophius piscatorius- — which live on the seafloor in relatively shallow coastal waters. Monkfish is prized in cooking mostly for its tail meat, which is the part typically sold and eaten. Texture and flavor: It has a firm, dense, meaty texture — often compared to lobster — with a mild, slightly sweet flavor. This has earned it the nickname "poor man's lobster."

Kamut -a trademarked name for Khorasan wheat- is an ancient grain with roots in the Fertile Crescent, popularized in the U.S. after seeds were reportedly brought over from Egypt in the mid-20th century, though its "King Tut's tomb" origin story is more legend than fact. It has a rich, buttery, nutty flavor with a firm, chewy texture, and its grains are notably large—up to twice the size of modern wheat kernels—making it popular in pastas, breads, and cereals. Kamut contains gluten but is prized for its higher protein and mineral content compared to common wheat, offering good levels of selenium, zinc, magnesium, and antioxidants.

description.en: Kanpyo is a Japanese ingredient made from dried strips of gourd — specifically the flesh of the calabash or bottle gourd -a variety called yūgao, related to what's sometimes called "bottle gourd" or "calabash" in English-. To make it, the gourd is peeled into long, thin ribbons, then sun-dried until they become firm, chewy strips. Before use, the dried strips are rehydrated and usually simmered in a mixture of soy sauce, sugar, and mirin -or dashi- until they turn a light brown color and take on a sweet-savory flavor.

description.en: A hickory nut is the edible nut produced by trees in the genus Carya — the same genus that includes pecans. They're native mostly to North America, with a few species in Asia. Encased in a thick, husk-like outer covering that splits open -fully or partially, depending on species- when ripe, revealing a hard shell. Inside that shell is the actual nutmeat. Flavor varies a lot by species — some, like shagbark hickory, are sweet and rich -similar to a pecan, which makes sense given the family connection-, while others, like pignut hickory, can be bitter or astringent.

description.en: Tilefish is a type of saltwater fish found mainly in the western Atlantic Ocean, from the northeastern U.S. down through the Gulf of Mexico. There are a few species, but the most commonly eaten ones are golden tilefish -also called "white tilefish" in markets- and blueline tilefish. Flavor and texture: Mild, sweet flavor with firm, moist flesh — often compared to a cross between lobster and crab in taste, which is why it's sometimes nicknamed "poor man's lobster." The texture holds up well to various cooking methods. Cooking methods: It works well baked, roasted, pan-seared, grilled, or poached. The skin can be crisped up nicely in a pan. It's popular in Japanese cuisine too, where it's called amadai and often prepared with the scales left on and fried until crispy.

Oligofructose is a type of fructan—a short-chain fructose oligosaccharide—found naturally in plants like chicory root, onions, and bananas, and produced commercially mainly through partial enzymatic hydrolysis of chicory inulin, a process developed in Europe where chicory-based fibers are widely used. It has a mild sweetness, roughly 30-50% as sweet as sucrose, with a clean flavor and no notable aroma, and is used in food products as a low-calorie sweetener, fat replacer, and texture enhancer. Unlike simple sugars, oligofructose acts as a soluble prebiotic fiber that resists digestion in the small intestine and ferments in the colon, feeding beneficial gut bacteria while providing fewer calories than sucrose and supporting digestive health.

It has an intensely savory, umami-rich flavor with notes reminiscent of broth or bouillon, and comes as a fine powder or paste used in tiny quantities to boost taste. Commonly used in soups, sauces, snack seasonings, and processed foods as a cheaper alternative to natural flavor development, HVP contributes free glutamic acid -similar to MSG- along with trace amino acids, but is used in such small amounts that it offers negligible nutritional value beyond flavor enhancement.

Carnitine is a quaternary ammonium compound involved in metabolism in most mammals, plants and some bacteria. The body synthesizes enough carnitine from lysine side chains to keep up with the needs of energy production in the body as carnitine acts as a transporter of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria to be oxidized and produce energy. Food sources rich in L-carnitine are animal products such as meat, poultry, fish, and milk. Redder meats tend to have higher levels of L-carnitine. Some individuals with genetic or medical disorders -like preterm infants- cannot make enough, so this makes carnitine a conditionally essential nutrient for them.

description.en: Cottonseed is the seed of the cotton plant -genus Gossypium-, harvested as a byproduct of cotton fiber production. After cotton bolls are picked, the fluffy fiber -lint- is separated from the seeds during a process called ginning. Each cotton boll contains several seeds embedded in the fiber. Raw cottonseed contains a natural compound called gossypol, which is toxic to humans in significant quantities. description.en: "White-flowered gourd" -calabash- refers to Lagenaria siceraria — also known as bottle gourd, calabash gourd, opo squash, or long melon. It's the same plant whose hard-shelled fruits are dried and used as bottles, bowls, or musical instruments, but when eaten as food it's harvested young and tender, before the shell hardens. Very mild, slightly sweet, with a texture similar to zucchini or chayote — it takes on the flavor of whatever it's cooked with. Common in cuisines: South Asian -India, Pakistan, Bangladesh — called lauki, doodhi, or ghiya-, Chinese -hu lu-, Vietnamese, Italian -cucuzza-, and West African cooking. One caution worth knowing: bottle gourds can occasionally develop high levels of cucurbitacins -the compound that makes some gourds bitter-, which can cause food poisoning. The rule of thumb is — if it tastes bitter, don't eat it, even if just one bite.

description.en: Sugar -sucrose- comes from sugarcane, first domesticated in New Guinea thousands of years ago and later spread through Asia and the Middle East to become the dominant global source, and from sugar beet, which took hold in Europe after Napoleon's early 1800s Continental Blockade cut off cane sugar imports and spurred domestic beet production, making it the region's primary source today. It has a pure, intensely sweet flavor with no notable aroma, available in forms ranging from fine granulated and powdered sugar to coarser raw and brown sugars with mild molasses notes. Used universally in baking, cooking, preserving, and sweetening beverages, sugar provides purely empty calories with no meaningful vitamins, minerals, or fiber, making it a source of energy without nutritional value.

description.en: Sweet corn is a cultivar of maize -Zea mays var. saccharata- bred to accumulate higher natural sugar content, harvested young and tender before the kernels mature and starch fully develops. Compared to local field maize, it has a distinctly sweeter, juicier taste with a crisp, tender bite. Popular worldwide, sweet corn is boiled or steamed on the cob, grilled, or used kernel-off-cob in salads, soups, stir-fries, and Indian street snacks like corn chaat. Nutritionally, it offers dietary fiber, carbohydrates, and moderate protein, along with vitamin C, B vitamins -especially folate-, magnesium, and antioxidants such as lutein and zeaxanthin, which support eye health. Its natural sweetness also makes it a favorite in both savory and lightly sweetened preparations.

description.en: Swordfish is a large, fast-swimming ocean fish -Xiphias gladius- known for the long, flat, sword-like bill it uses to slash at prey. As food, it's prized for a few distinct qualities: Texture and flavor: The flesh is firm, meaty, and dense — often compared to a good steak more than to flakier white fish. The flavor is mild but slightly rich, with a subtle sweetness; Cut and cooking: It's usually sold as thick steaks rather than fillets, since the loin is large. It grills, broils, or pan-sears very well, and holds up on skewers -it's a common choice for kebabs-; Fat content: It's a moderately fatty fish, which helps keep it moist during high-heat cooking like grilling — unlike very lean white fish that dry out easily.

description.en: Caseinate is a soluble form of casein—typically sodium or calcium caseinate—created by treating milk casein with an alkali to make it water-soluble, a processing method developed in the early-to-mid 20th century to allow casein's functional properties to be used more easily in manufactured foods. It has a neutral, mildly milky flavor with no strong aroma, and unlike regular casein, it dissolves smoothly in liquids and forms stable emulsions rather than clumping into curds. Widely used as an emulsifier and protein fortifier in coffee creamers, processed cheeses, and protein supplements, caseinate remains a complete protein containing all nine essential amino acids, along with calcium and phosphorus from its dairy origin.

description.en: Water is a naturally occurring compound of hydrogen and oxygen, found throughout the environment in oceans, rivers, lakes, and groundwater, and sourced for consumption from municipal supplies, wells, springs, and glaciers depending on region. It has a neutral, essentially flavorless and odorless profile, though mineral content can lend subtle differences—spring water often tastes slightly mineral-rich, while distilled water tastes notably flat. As the foundation of virtually all food and beverage preparation, water contains no calories, protein, fat, or carbohydrates, though mineral or spring varieties may carry trace amounts of minerals like calcium, magnesium, and potassium, and it remains essential for nearly every bodily function.

A pili nut -Canarium ovatum- is a tropical tree nut native to the Philippines, particularly grown in the Bicol region. The nut has a rich, buttery flavor and texture, often compared to a cross between an almond and a macadamia nut — but generally considered even richer and more delicate. They're eaten raw, roasted, or candied, and are also used in pastries, pesto-style sauces, and as a snack food. In the Philippines they're a popular treat, especially when sugar-coated.

description.en: Cocoa comes from the seeds -beans- of the cacao tree, native to Central and South America and used by the Aztecs and Maya for thousands of years in ceremonial and medicinal drinks long before it spread to Europe in the 16th century and became the basis for modern chocolate. It has a rich, bitter, complex flavor with earthy, fruity, and slightly astringent notes that vary by origin and processing, and comes in forms ranging from raw beans and nibs to fine cocoa powder, defined by its fat content -cocoa butter- after pressing. Used in chocolate-making, baking, and beverages, cocoa is notably rich in flavanol antioxidants, along with magnesium, iron, and fiber, though its bitter compounds are often offset with added sugar in most commercial products.

description.en: Soft wheat has been cultivated for millennia, with whole-grain flour production expanding globally as milling techniques evolved to preserve the bran and germ. Its lower protein and gluten content make it ideal for tender baked goods like cakes, pastries, cookies, and flatbreads rather than yeasted bread. Nutritionally, it retains more fiber, B vitamins, and minerals than refined flour, thanks to the whole grain remaining intact.

description.en: Spelt is an ancient wheat variety that originated in the Near East and was widely cultivated across Europe, particularly Germany and Switzerland, from the Bronze Age until being largely displaced by modern wheat. It has a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor with a tender yet chewy texture, used much like wheat in bread, pasta, and baked goods, often prized for its more digestible protein structure. Spelt does contain gluten and offers a good source of fiber, protein, manganese, and B vitamins, along with more zinc and iron than common wheat.

description.en: Invert sugar is a liquid sugar syrup produced by splitting sucrose into its component parts—glucose and fructose—through hydrolysis using heat, acid, or enzymes, a process discovered in the 19th century and now widely used in food manufacturing rather than home kitchens. It has a flavor sweeter than regular sugar -since fructose tastes sweeter than sucrose- with a smooth, syrupy texture, and it's prized in baking and confectionery for resisting crystallization, retaining moisture, and extending shelf life in products like candies, jams, and soft baked goods. Like other sugars, invert sugar provides purely empty calories with no meaningful vitamins, minerals, or fiber, offering energy without nutritional value.

description.en: Samai, or little millet -Panicum sumatrense, syn. Panicum miliare-, is one of India's oldest cultivated minor millets, traditionally grown in the rain-fed hills and plateaus of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Odisha for over 5‚000 years. Its small, round grains carry a mild, subtly nutty flavor and light, fluffy texture when cooked. Valued for its resilience in poor soil and low rainfall, it's traditionally used as a rice substitute—steamed, boiled into porridge -kanji-, or ground into idli and dosa batters—and is popular during religious fasting periods. Nutritionally, samai is rich in dietary fiber, iron, and B vitamins, has a low glycemic index, and is naturally gluten-free, making it valued in diabetic-friendly and gluten-free diets.

comment.en: USDA NDB 20001 is a generic entry covering amaranth grain broadly -species like Amaranthus cruentus, hypochondriacus, or caudatus-, not specifically black-seeded varieties. "Black amaranth" usually refers to darker-seeded cultivars -sometimes ornamental/wild types like Amaranthus hybridus-, which can differ slightly in flavor -often described as more bitter/earthy than the common cream-colored grain amaranth- and are less commonly the ones used in commercial food products.

description.en: Native to Central and South America, amaranth was a staple grain of the Aztec and Inca civilizations, prized for its resilience and nutritional density. Black amaranth seeds have a mild, earthy, slightly peppery flavor with a subtle nuttiness that intensifies when toasted or popped. Versatile in the kitchen, they can be cooked like porridge, popped for snacking or garnishing, ground into flour for gluten-free baking, or sprouted for salads and bowls. Nutritionally, amaranth is a complete protein containing all nine essential amino acids, including lysine—rare among grains. It's also rich in fiber, iron, magnesium, and manganese, and naturally gluten-free, making it a nutrient-dense choice for ancient-grain and health-focused products.

description.en: Raising agents are substances added to baked goods to produce carbon dioxide gas and create rise and lightness, with early forms like yeast used since ancient Egyptian times, while chemical versions such as baking soda and baking powder were developed in the 19th century as faster, more reliable alternatives. They are essentially flavorless or very mildly bitter/metallic on their own, though excess use can leave a soapy or tinny aftertaste, and they work by releasing gas bubbles that get trapped in dough or batter, creating a light, airy texture. Used across breads, cakes, and pastries—commonly as baking soda, baking powder, yeast, or ammonium bicarbonate—raising agents are used in such small quantities that they contribute negligible calories or nutrients, functioning purely as a leavening tool rather than a nutritional ingredient.

description.en: Varagu, known in English as kodo millet, is another of India's ancient minor millets, cultivated for over 3‚000 years primarily in the drier, hilly regions of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, and Chhattisgarh. It's one of the hardiest millets, thriving in poor soils with minimal water, and is often grown as a famine-reserve or marginal-land crop. The small, round, reddish-brown grains have an earthy, mildly nutty flavor similar to other millets. Traditionally cooked like rice, ground into flour for flatbreads, or used in porridges and idli/dosa batters, it's also popular in fasting foods and diabetic-friendly diets. Nutritionally, kodo millet is notably high in dietary fiber and polyphenol antioxidants, a good source of iron and B vitamins, naturally gluten-free, and has one of the lowest glycemic indices among cereals.

description.en: CHORIZO or chouriço is a type of pork sausage. description.en: Choline chloride is an organic compound containing both quaternary ammonium salt and an alcohol. It is an important additive in feed especially for chickens where it accelerates growth. The US Food and Drug Administration requires that infant formula not made from cow's milk be supplemented with choline. Choline-providing dietary supplement ingredients include: choline chloride, choline bitartrate, citicoline -CDP-choline-, L-alpha-glycerophosphocholine -Alpha-GPC-, lecithin, phosphatidylcholine.

Agave syrup -or agave nectar- is a liquid sweetener extracted from the core of the agave plant, particularly Agave tequilana, with production centered in Mexico where the plant has long been used to make traditional sweeteners and beverages like pulque. It has a mild, neutral sweetness—often noted as sweeter than honey—with subtle caramel notes in darker varieties, and a thin, smooth, honey-like texture that dissolves easily in cold liquids. Popular as a vegan honey substitute in beverages, baking, and dressings, agave syrup is very high in fructose -often 70-90%-, giving it a low glycemic index despite being calorie-dense, though its fructose concentration has raised similar metabolic concerns as high-fructose corn syrup.

description.en: Isomaltooligosaccharide -IMO- is a short-chain carbohydrate composed of glucose units linked in branched α-1‚6 bonds, found in trace amounts in fermented foods like miso, soy sauce, and sake, and produced commercially through enzymatic conversion of starch, a technology pioneered and widely commercialized in Japan since the 1980s. It has a mild sweetness, roughly 40-60% as sweet as sucrose, with a clean flavor and syrupy texture similar to corn syrup, making it a popular sugar substitute in protein bars, baked goods, and "low-sugar" products. Marketed as a prebiotic fiber that partially resists digestion and supports gut bacteria, IMO provides fewer calories than sucrose, though recent research has questioned how much of it is truly fermented in the colon versus digested as regular glucose, making its fiber and metabolic benefits somewhat contested.

Carbonated water is water infused with dissolved carbon dioxide gas under pressure, either occurring naturally in mineral springs—historically prized in spa towns like Perrier in France—or produced artificially through mechanical carbonation, a process commercialized in the late 18th century. It has a neutral base flavor with a distinctive sharp, slightly acidic bite and effervescent tingle from the carbonic acid formed as CO2 dissolves, and a lively, fizzy texture that fades once opened. Used as a refreshing standalone drink, a mixer in cocktails, and a base for flavored sodas, carbonated water contains no calories, protein, fat, or carbohydrates, and offers the same trace minerals as its source water, with no meaningful nutritional difference from still water beyond the carbonation itself.

description.en: Epazote -Dysphania ambrosioides, formerly Chenopodium ambrosioides- is a pungent, aromatic herb widely used in Mexican and Central American cooking. The flavor is hard to pin down — people describe it as a mix of citrus, mint, anise, tar, and even petroleum-like notes. It's strong, so it's used in moderation, usually just a sprig or a few leaves per dish, added toward the end of cooking to preserve its aroma. Epazote contains compounds -like ascaridole- that can be toxic in concentrated amounts, such as in essential oil form. Using fresh or dried leaves in normal cooking quantities is considered safe and is how it's traditionally consumed — but it shouldn't be consumed as a concentrated extract or in medicinal "high dose" preparations.

description.en: Fiddlehead ferns are the tightly coiled, immature fronds of certain fern species, harvested in early spring before they unfurl. They're named for their resemblance to the curled end -scroll- of a fiddle or violin. Most common edible variety: Ostrich fern -Matteuccia struthiopteris- is the safest and most widely eaten species. Not all fern fiddleheads are edible — some are toxic, so identification matters. Often described as a cross between asparagus, green beans, and a slightly nutty, grassy taste. Fiddleheads must be cooked thoroughly -boiled or steamed for several minutes, then sautéed if desired- before eating. Raw or undercooked fiddleheads have caused foodborne illness outbreaks — they can carry bacteria or contain compounds that cause nausea, cramps, and diarrhea if not properly prepared.

description.en: MALTOSE, also known as maltobiose or malt sugar, is a disaccharide formed from two units of glucose joined. Maltose is a component of malt, a substance which is obtained in the process of allowing grain to soften in water and germinate. It is also present in highly variable quantities in partially hydrolysed starch products like maltodextrin, corn syrup and acid-thinned starch. In humans, maltose is broken down by various maltase enzymes, providing two glucose molecules which can be further processed: either broken down to provide energy, or stored as glycogen. The lack of the sucrase-isomaltase enzyme in humans causes sucrose intolerance.

description.en: Ice is water in its solid state, forming when temperatures drop to or below 0°C -32°F-, found naturally in glaciers, polar regions, and frost, and produced commercially or at home through refrigeration for use in food and beverages. It has no flavor or aroma of its own, taking on a hard, crystalline texture that can range from clear and dense to cloudy and brittle depending on freezing speed and mineral content. Used primarily for chilling drinks and food, preserving perishables, and in ice sculptures or winter sports, ice contains no calories, protein, fat, or carbohydrates, offering the same trace minerals as its source water but purely a physical, non-nutritive ingredient.

description.en: Trehalose is a naturally occurring disaccharide made of two glucose molecules, found in trace amounts in mushrooms, honey, and various plants and insects, and produced commercially today mainly through enzymatic conversion of starch, largely pioneered by Japanese researchers in the 1990s who made large-scale production affordable. It has a mild sweetness—roughly 45% as sweet as sucrose—with no notable aroma, and is valued in food processing for its exceptional stability, ability to protect texture and moisture in frozen or dried foods, and resistance to browning at high heat. Used in baked goods, frozen desserts, and dried fruits as a stabilizer and mild sweetener, trehalose provides purely empty calories with no meaningful vitamins, minerals, or fiber, though it's digested more slowly than sucrose, giving it a gentler effect on blood sugar.

description.en: Glucose is a simple sugar -monosaccharide- that occurs naturally in fruits, honey, and plants, and is produced commercially by breaking down starch—typically from corn in the U.S. or wheat and potatoes in Europe—through enzymatic or acid hydrolysis. description.en: Nutritional yeast is a deactivated form of Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast, typically grown on molasses and then heat-killed before being dried into flakes or powder, popularized in the mid-20th century as a health food, particularly within vegan and vegetarian communities. It has a distinctly savory, cheesy, nutty flavor with umami depth, making it a popular seasoning sprinkled over popcorn, pasta, and salads or blended into vegan cheese sauces. Unlike active baking yeast, it has no leavening power since it's deactivated, but it stands out nutritionally as a complete protein source rich in B vitamins—often fortified with B12—making it especially valued in plant-based diets for filling that typical nutritional gap.

Dock -genus Rumex, especially curly dock — Rumex crispus — and broad-leaved dock — Rumex obtusifolius- is a wild edible plant. Young leaves have a tart, lemony, slightly sour flavor thanks to oxalic acid — similar to sorrel but a bit milder. As leaves mature they get tougher and more bitter/astringent. Young leaves: eaten raw in salads, or added to soups, stews, and sautés like spinach.; Older leaves: usually cooked -boiled or braised- to mellow the sourness and soften the texture.

description.en: Protein is a macronutrient made of amino acid chains, sourced from a wide range of foods—animal sources like meat, fish, eggs, and dairy, and plant sources like legumes, grains, nuts, and soy—with humans relying on food-derived protein since prehistoric times as one of the three core macronutrients alongside fats and carbohydrates. Its flavor and texture vary enormously by source, from the rich, savory taste of meats to the neutral, often bland profile of isolated protein powders, which are typically processed from whey, soy, or pea into fine, mixable forms. Essential for building and repairing muscle, enzymes, and hormones, protein is measured by its amino acid completeness—animal proteins and a few plant sources like quinoa and soy are "complete," containing all nine essential amino acids, while most other plant proteins must be combined to achieve the same profile.

description.en: Tapioca pearls are made from cassava root starch, a plant native to South America but now cultivated widely across Brazil, Southeast Asia, and Africa. On their own, dry pearls are essentially flavorless and starchy, taking on a mild sweetness and chewy, translucent texture once cooked. They're most commonly used in bubble tea, puddings, and Southeast Asian desserts, or as a thickener in soups and pie fillings. Nutritionally, tapioca is mostly pure carbohydrate with very little protein, fiber, or micronutrients, making it a gluten-free energy source but not a significant source of other nutrients.

Juniper berry sauce is often a popular flavoring choice for quail, pheasant, veal, rabbit, venison and other game dishes.

description.en: Berries are small, fleshy, typically sweet-tart fruits produced by a wide range of flowering plants, growing wild across temperate and cold regions worldwide long before cultivation, with varieties like strawberries, blueberries, raspberries, and blackberries becoming widely farmed staples in Europe and North America. They have a flavor ranging from intensely sweet to sharply tart, often balanced with floral or earthy notes, and a soft, juicy texture that varies from the delicate burst of raspberries to the firmer bite of blueberries. Eaten fresh, dried, or used in jams, baking, and beverages, berries are notably rich in antioxidants -especially anthocyanins-, fiber, and vitamin C, making them among the most nutrient-dense fruits.

Sourdough is a naturally leavened bread made using a fermented starter of wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria rather than commercial yeast, a method dating back thousands of years to ancient Egypt and still central to regional baking traditions like San Francisco's tangy loaves. It has a distinctive tangy, slightly sour flavor with a chewy, dense crumb and crisp, often blistered crust, shaped by the specific microbial culture of its starter, which can vary by region and even household. Made simply from flour, water, salt, and the starter culture, sourdough's slow fermentation is thought to improve digestibility and lower the glycemic impact compared to conventionally leavened bread, while offering fiber, B vitamins, and modest protein from the flour base.

description.lt: Stabilizatoriai – medžiagos, padedančios išlaikyti pastovią fizinę ir cheminę maisto produkto būseną; stabilizatoriai apima medžiagas, padedančias išlaikyti dviejų ir daugiau nesimaišančių medžiagų vienalytę dispersiją maisto produkte, taip pat medžiagas, stabilizuojančias, išlaikančias ar sustiprinančias maisto produkto esamą spalvą, ir medžiagas, padidinančias maisto rišamąsias savybes, įskaitant baltymų skersinius ryšius, padedančius atskiras maisto dalis apjungti į atskirą naujai pagamintą produktą.
description.es: Estabilizantes: sustancias que posibilitan el mantenimiento del estado físico-químico de un producto alimenticio; incluyen las sustancias que permiten el mantenimiento de una dispersión homogénea de dos o más sustancias no miscibles en un producto alimenticio, las que estabilizan, retienen o intensifican el color de un producto alimenticio y las que incrementan la capacidad de enlace de los alimentos, en especial el entrecruzamiento de las proteínas, que permite unir trozos de alimento para formar un alimento reconstituido.
description.en: Stabilisers are substances which make it possible to maintain the physico-chemical state of a foodstuff; stabilisers include substances which enable the maintenance of a homogenous dispersion of two or more immiscible substances in a foodstuff, substances which stabilise, retain or intensify an existing colour of a foodstuff and substances which increase the binding capacity of the food, including the formation of cross-links between proteins enabling the binding of food pieces into re-constituted food.
description.it: Gli stabilizzanti sono sostanze che rendono possibile il mantenimento dello stato fisico-chimico di un prodotto alimentare; gli stabilizzanti comprendono le sostanze che rendono possibile il mantenimento di una dispersione omogenea di due o più sostanze immiscibili in un prodotto alimentare, le sostanze che stabilizzano, trattengono o intensificano la colorazione esistente di un prodotto alimentare e le sostanze che aumentano la capacità degli alimenti di formare legami, compresa la formazione di legami incrociati tra le proteine tale da consentire il legame delle particelle per la formazione dell'alimento ricostituito.
description.fi: Stabilointiaineet ovat aineita, jotka mahdollistavat elintarvikkeen fyysis-kemiallisen tilan ylläpitämisen; stabilointiaineisiin kuuluu aineita, jotka mahdollistavat kahdesta tai useammasta sekoittumattomasta aineesta muodostetun tasaisen seoksen säilymisen elintarvikkeessa, aineita, jotka stabiloivat, ylläpitävät tai vahvistavat elintarvikkeen olemassa olevaa väriä, ja aineita, jotka lisäävät elintarvikkeen sitoutumiskykyä, mukaan luettuna ristisidosten muodostuminen proteiinien välille niin, että elintarvikkeen osat voidaan sitoa ennastetuksi elintarvikkeeksi.
description.et: Stabilisaatorid – ained, mis võimaldavad säilitada toidu füüsikalis-keemilist olekut; stabilisaatorite hulka kuuluvad ained, mis võimaldavad säilitada kahe või enama segunematu aine ühtlast dispergeerumist toidus ning toidu värvust stabiliseerivad, säilitavad või tugevdavad ained, samuti ained, mis suurendavad toidu sidumisvõimet, k.a valkudevaheliste võrkstruktuuride teket, mis võimaldab siduda toidu osi taastatud toiduks.
description.pt: Estabilizadores: substâncias que tornam possível a manutenção do estado físico-químico dos géneros alimentícios. Os estabilizadores incluem as substâncias que permitem a manutenção de uma dispersão homogénea de duas ou mais substâncias imiscíveis nos géneros alimentícios, as substâncias que estabilizam, retêm ou intensificam a cor natural dos géneros alimentícios e as substâncias que aumentam a capacidade de aglomeração do género alimentício, incluindo a formação de ligações cruzadas entre proteínas que permitem a aglomeração dos elementos alimentares para a formação de um género alimentício reconstituído.
description.nl: Stabilisatoren: stoffen die het mogelijk maken de fysisch-chemische toestand van een levensmiddel te handhaven; stabilisatoren omvatten stoffen die het mogelijk maken een homogene dispersie van twee of meer onmengbare stoffen in een levensmiddel te handhaven, stoffen die een bestaande kleur van een levensmiddel stabiliseren, fixeren of intensifiëren en stoffen die het bindend vermogen van het levensmiddel vergroten, onder meer door de vorming van crosslinks tussen eiwitten waardoor afzonderlijke deeltjes tot een gereconstitueerd levensmiddel worden gebonden.

description.fr: Les stabilisants sont des substances qui, ajoutées à une denrée alimentaire, permettent de maintenir son état physico-chimique. L-CARNITINE is the left isomer of carnitine, a quaternary ammonium compound involved in metabolism in most mammals, plants and some bacteria. The body synthesizes enough carnitine from lysine side chains to keep up with the needs of energy production in the body as carnitine acts as a transporter of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria to be oxidized and produce energy. Food sources rich in L-carnitine are animal products such as meat, poultry, fish, and milk. Redder meats tend to have higher levels of L-carnitine. Some individuals with genetic or medical disorders -like preterm infants- cannot make enough, so this makes carnitine a conditionally essential nutrient for them.

description.en: Rolled oats are whole oat groats that have been steamed and pressed flat with large rollers, a processing method developed in the late 1800s to shorten cooking time while keeping the grain mostly intact. They have a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor with a soft, chewy texture that holds its shape better than instant oats, making them the classic choice for traditional oatmeal, granola, and baking. description.en: Brewing water is water specifically treated or selected for beer or coffee production, with mineral content—calcium, magnesium, sulfate, chloride, and bicarbonate—carefully adjusted to match regional styles, a practice tracing back to historic brewing centers like Burton-on-Trent -high sulfate, favoring hoppy pale ales- and Pilsen -very soft water, ideal for delicate lagers-. It has a neutral base flavor, but its mineral balance subtly shapes the final beverage's taste—sulfate accentuates hop bitterness and dryness, while chloride enhances malt sweetness and mouthfeel. Used as the primary ingredient in brewing -making up roughly 90-95% of beer-, water's mineral profile is often adjusted through filtration, dilution, or targeted mineral additions to achieve consistency and match desired beer or coffee styles. As with plain water, brewing water contains no calories, protein, fat, or carbohydrates, only trace minerals that influence flavor rather than nutrition.

description.en: Fructooligosaccharide -FOS- is a short-chain fructan found naturally in foods like chicory root, onions, garlic, and bananas, and produced commercially either by extracting it from chicory or through enzymatic conversion of sucrose, with much of the technology developed in Japan and France. It has a mild sweetness, roughly 30-50% as sweet as sucrose, with a clean flavor and no notable aroma, and is used in food products as a low-calorie sweetener, texture enhancer, and fat replacer. Like oligofructose, FOS acts as a soluble prebiotic fiber that resists digestion in the small intestine and ferments in the colon to feed beneficial gut bacteria, providing fewer calories than sucrose while supporting digestive health.

Vital wheat gluten is a concentrated protein extracted from wheat flour by washing away the starch, a process refined industrially in the 20th century to create a versatile baking additive. On its own it's bland and neutral in flavor, though it develops a chewy, meaty texture when hydrated and cooked. It's used to boost elasticity and rise in bread dough, and is a key ingredient in seitan and other plant-based meat substitutes. Nutritionally, it's exceptionally high in protein -over 75%- with very little fat or carbohydrate, though as pure gluten it's unsuitable for those with gluten intolerance or celiac disease.
